column6: Moses sets life and death before Israel and commands “choose life”; this gives the commentary’s claim about choosing the better end a covenantal, present-tense counterpart, without making the choice an afterlife doctrine.
Joseph says God sent him ahead to preserve a remnant and keep many alive; this makes survival a gift of providence, while the famine remnant is not itself the commentary’s morally good remnant.

After the transgression, God prevents the humans from eating from the tree of life and living forever; Genesis treats unending earthly life as something to guard against, unlike the commentary’s promised better later life.

column5: God’s power over life and Sheol
column6: Hannah says the LORD kills and makes alive, bringing down to Sheol and raising up; this gives a concrete scriptural form to the commentary’s claim that lasting life belongs to God.

“Better is the end of a matter than its beginning” joins Hebrew ʾaḥarit (end, later outcome), cognate with Arabic ākhirah, to טוב (good); the verse states the commentary’s better-later comparison without referring specifically to afterlife.

The proverb says there is an ʾaḥarit, a future or latter outcome, and one’s hope will not be cut off; the Hebrew after-root and its hope context illuminate the commentary’s awaited, good, enduring future.

The messenger says the vision concerns what will happen to Daniel’s people in the latter days; Hebrew ʾaḥarit and Arabic ākhirah share the after-root, here naming an eschatological future rather than the afterlife itself.

Job’s redeemer “at the last” uses the Hebrew after-root related to Arabic ākhirah and voices hope beyond present ruin; whether Job means a postmortem vision is disputed, so the lexical link is firmer than the doctrinal one.

The LORD calls himself “first” and “last” and denies another God; Hebrew ʾaḥaron corresponds to Arabic ākhir, while the verse places the whole sequence under divine sovereignty as the commentary does.
In the Song of Moses God swears, “I live forever”; this grounds the commentary’s distinction between creatures that perish and the One who alone possesses enduring life.
Isaiah names the high and exalted one as dwelling in eternity; this gives a direct counterpart to the commentary’s account of permanence as belonging to God, not to life independently of God.

The prophet compares all flesh to grass and its beauty to a field flower; this recalls the commentary’s pasture that greens and then becomes dry refuse, making present life’s real beauty yet transience visible.
The grass withers and the flower falls, but God’s word stands forever; this directly pairs the commentary’s decaying vegetation with what remains, while locating permanence in divine speech.
Rain and snow water earth so it sprouts and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; the verse supplies the commentary’s concrete rain-to-growth scene and connects waiting to provision.

The rain image continues as God’s word goes out and accomplishes what God intends; alongside the commentary’s expected rain and lasting good, the verse makes the awaited outcome effective rather than merely delayed.

Isaiah calls the dead to awake and sing, with dew on the dust; this is a direct resurrection counterpart to the commentary’s later life as the fuller life, and its dew also meets the surah’s rain-and-growth imagery.

Daniel says sleepers in the dust awake, some to everlasting life and others to shame; this sharply matches the commentary’s point that duration alone is not good, since lasting life and lasting disgrace diverge.

The wise and those who lead many to righteousness shine like stars forever; the verse gives a concrete image of enduring honor and differentiated standing in the future order described in the commentary.
Heavens vanish and earth wears out, but God’s salvation is forever; this makes the commentary’s contrast between perishable present life and enduring good explicit in a single prophetic scene.

This midrash reads the creation verdict “very good” as including death; beside the commentary’s insistence that lasting existence must also be good, it warns that goodness and mere survival cannot be collapsed.

The Mishnah calls this world a vestibule before the World-to-Come and urges preparation there; it makes the commentary’s present choice and later arrival a practical sequence, not two unrelated realms.

Rabbi Yaakov says one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world outweighs the World-to-Come, yet one hour of its bliss outweighs all this life; this preserves present good while ranking future joy higher, just as the commentary does.

The sages picture the World-to-Come without eating, drinking, trade, or rivalry, with the righteous enjoying the divine presence; this interprets later life as a different and lasting good rather than an extension of current consumption.

The Talmud teaches that the reward for commandments is not paid out in this world; this gives a rabbinic account of why the better recompense may be delayed and why immediate prosperity is not the measure of good.
The souls of the righteous are in God’s hand and no torment touches them; this presents postmortem life as secure in God, corresponding to the commentary’s claim that permanence rests with its giver.
The dead may seem punished, but their hope is full of immortality; this directly joins the commentary’s hope for what comes later to a life that endures.
After their trial the righteous shine and judge nations; this supplies a specific image of lasting honor and rank, not simply survival, for the commentary’s differentiated future.
The righteous live forever and their reward is with the Lord; this directly connects enduring life with good and locates its source in God, as the commentary’s two predicates do.
A tortured brother says the King of the universe will raise them to everlasting renewal of life; this is a direct resurrection counterpart to the commentary’s later, enduring life.

The brother tells the king that there will be no resurrection to life for him; the scene makes the later life a moral distinction, while the commentary’s claim is framed as a choice between better and worse ends.
The mother tells her sons that the Creator will give back their breath and life; this grounds lasting life in the Creator’s power, matching the commentary’s insistence that permanence is granted.
Jesus warns that earthly treasure is eaten by moth and rust; this gives a concrete instance of the commentary’s claim that present goods have value but do not remain.
Jesus directs hearers to store treasure in heaven where it is not destroyed; this directly ranks a lasting good above goods exposed to decay, as the commentary’s comparison does.
Jesus says the heart follows one’s treasure; this connects the commentary’s deliberate preference for the near life with the practical consequence of what a person chooses to value.

In the parable, worldly anxiety and wealth’s deceitfulness choke the word so it bears no fruit; this links the commentary’s vegetation imagery to a present-world attachment that prevents lasting good.
Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one’s life; this sharply states the commentary’s reversal of a choice that treats immediate gain as the better end.
Jesus tells the rich man to sell his possessions, give to the poor, have treasure in heaven, and follow him; the promised lasting good is placed directly before someone attached to present wealth.
The rich man goes away grieving because he has many possessions; his response makes the commentary’s knowingly choosing the visible present over a better future concrete.
The rich man plans to store goods for many years and relax; this is a specific picture of assigning permanence to present abundance, the very false security the commentary contests.
God tells the rich man he will die that night, so his stored goods cannot secure his future; this makes the commentary’s contrast between transient possession and what remains concrete.
Jesus tells disciples to give alms and make purses that do not wear out, with unfailing treasure in heaven; this closely matches present goods exchanged for a durable good.
Jesus says the heart will be where one’s treasure is; this adds the commentary’s choice-and-preference dimension to the contrast between earthly and lasting goods.

column5: invited guests choose their own plans
column6: The first invited guest excuses himself to inspect a field; the banquet already offered is set aside for an immediate possession, concretizing the commentary’s knowingly preferring what is near.
Another guest prioritizes testing five yoke of oxen over the prepared feast; the second concrete excuse shows how material opportunity can displace a better offer already in view.

Abraham tells the rich man he received good things during life while Lazarus now receives comfort; this preserves the commentary’s nuance that present life has real good, yet the later order reverses its priority.

column5: food that perishes and food enduring
column6: Jesus contrasts perishable food with food enduring to eternal life; this directly joins the commentary’s material provision imagery to the choice of what lasts.

column5: life in this world and eternal life
column6: Jesus says the one who loves life in this world loses it, while the one who gives it up keeps it for eternal life; this states the commentary’s near/later reversal in an ethical form.
Paul describes those who persist in good work seeking glory, honor, and immortality as receiving eternal life; this directly joins goodness, endurance, and the future reward in the commentary.
Paul contrasts athletes’ perishable wreath with the imperishable crown sought by disciplined runners; this meets the commentary’s race image and its point about reserving effort for the lasting end.
Paul says the sun, moon, and stars differ in glory; in the resurrection argument this gives a concrete analogue for the commentary’s claim that the later life has its own degrees of rank.
The body sown perishable is raised imperishable; this answers the commentary’s contrast between a changing pasture and a life that remains in its renewed state.
Paul says the mortal must put on immortality; this makes enduring life a granted transformation, consonant with the commentary’s claim that permanence belongs to God to give.
Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal; this gives the commentary’s near-versus-later ranking a clear temporal and epistemic form.

column5: sowing to Spirit and eternal life
column6: Paul contrasts sowing to the flesh, which reaps corruption, with sowing to the Spirit, which reaps eternal life; this joins agricultural harvest to the choice between decay and enduring good.
Paul urges persistence in doing good because a harvest comes at the proper time; this supplies the commentary’s image of waiting for a good outcome that arrives later.

The believers accept the seizure of their property because they know they have a better and abiding possession; this is an exceptionally close formulation of present loss weighed against lasting good.
The following verse warns them not to throw away their confidence, which has a great reward; it makes the commentary’s deferred reward something to await rather than abandon for immediate relief.
The author says endurance is needed to receive what God promised; this gives the later good a temporal sequence and links waiting with faithful action.
Moses chooses mistreatment with God’s people rather than the temporary pleasure of sin; this is a direct example of refusing immediate enjoyment for a better future allegiance.
Moses considers reproach greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures because he looks to the reward; this concretely revalues present riches in light of a later good.

column5: hope not set on uncertain riches
column6: Paul tells the rich not to hope in uncertain wealth but in God, who richly provides; this recognizes material goods as real provision while refusing them the permanence the commentary reserves for God.
The wealthy are told to do good, be generous, and ready to share; this gives ethical content to the commentary’s “good” that remains, rather than treating permanence alone as sufficient.
Such generosity stores up treasure for the future and takes hold of true life; this directly joins present action, later reward, and the fuller life the commentary describes.
Peter describes an inheritance kept in heaven as imperishable, undefiled, and unfading; this closely matches the commentary’s claim that the later good remains in its first state.

John says the world and its desire pass away, while the one doing God’s will remains forever; this is a direct ethical and temporal counterpart to the commentary’s contrast between transient preference and lasting good.
Jesus distinguishes eternal life from eternal punishment; this supports the commentary’s insistence that permanence by itself is not good and that the lasting outcome must also be judged.
The new creation has no more death, mourning, crying, or pain; this offers a concrete picture of later life as good and enduring, unlike merely remaining in a state without life.
